source.title: FlatNAS: optimizing Flatness in Neural Architecture Search for Out-of-Distribution Robustness
source.authors: Matteo Gambella; Fabrizio Pittorino; Manuel Roveri

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The first results table is flattened and its caption is not adjacent to its values; the paper identifies it as Table I in the surrounding text.
record.tranche_reason: Uses SAM and a weight-perturbation robustness metric to search for architectures with improved OOD corruption robustness. It does not test the listed claims about in-distribution train-test generalization gaps.
record.gate_note: The reported experiments compare clean CIFAR test error, weight-perturbation robustness R(x, σ), and corruption error mCE. These results concern OOD corruption robustness; they do not measure the in-distribution train-test gap named by the claim versions. The row results are described under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: FlatNAS uses magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation robustness and sharpness-aware optimization to improve NAS performance. It reports clean classification error and corruption error, but no training–test generalization gaps or comparison of generalization-measure rankings required by V7. Its other experiments do not test V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that sharpness-aware methods can enhance corruption robustness in parameter-constrained NAS and alter the architectures selected. Their strongest results use α=0.5; they acknowledge degraded outcomes at α=0.1 and results comparable to CNAS followed by SAM at α=0.9.
record.recipe_differences: The study conducts constrained neural architecture search using an OFA MobileNetV3 supernet, adaptive SAM, and a weight-perturbation robustness objective, then evaluates corruption robustness. It does not reproduce the claim versions' experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report different outcomes by dataset, α setting, and optimizer comparison. They state α=0.5 gives better mCE, α=0.1 worsens clean accuracy and mCE, and α=0.9 is comparable to CNAS followed by SAM. Corruption intensity also varies in the figures.

fits_no_version.finding: At α=0.5, FlatNAS reduces mCE relative to CNAS from 34.58 to 26.58 on CIFAR-10-C and from 53.93 to 48.71 on CIFAR-100-C. At α=0.1, mCE instead rises to 35.26 and 56.35 despite lower weight-perturbation error increases than CNAS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jointly optimizing clean accuracy and magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation robustness during constrained NAS can improve corruption robustness, with outcomes dependent on objective weighting.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Network
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the table values. The first results table is flattened in the supplied text. The experiments evaluate corruption robustness rather than in-distribution train-test generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for 1−FA(x), parameter count, MACs, or corruption-type-specific results. The clean error and model-size values are included in the existing row notes/size fields; corruption-type results are shown in Figures 4 and 5 without recoverable numerical values in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the coexistence of memorization capacity with natural-label generalization.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive gradient methods versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; recovery through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.

Whether magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranks training–test gaps among similarly fitted networks, including comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Neither training errors nor generalization gaps are reported.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: R measures the average increase in training error under multiplicative Gaussian weight perturbations at σ=0.05, averaged over 20 samples; lower values indicate greater tolerance. It is not a training–test gap. All ten rows are method-performance comparisons and should remain outside the evidence rows for V1–V8. No uncertainty estimates accompany the table values.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization.
Test error across network widths beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance under tuning.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Whether magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance tracks the in-distribution train-test gap.
Whether removing memorized training examples lowers test accuracy.
